title: How the Bible was gathered
hook: letters passed hand to hand and read aloud, until the churches knew which books were theirs

segments.voice: Yesterday, four sides: scripture, tradition, reason and experience. Your line was four sides of a question. Which side did you find you usually skip? Day one thousand sixty-five.

At the end of a letter to a small church in Colossae, Paul adds a note about the mail. When this letter has been read to you, he says, send it on to the church at Laodicea, and make sure you read the one coming from Laodicea too. So: a scroll, read aloud to a room of people, then rolled up and carried down the road to the next room. That's the Bible before it was a book. Letters and gospels, passed hand to hand, read out loud in worship. Today: how all of that became one book. How the Bible was gathered.

The Bible didn't arrive as a bound volume. Luke's Gospel opens by admitting there were other accounts: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." Many. Luke wasn't the only one writing, and the churches had to come to know which writings were theirs. Christians often describe it the way Paul's note suggests: by reading. The writings that churches kept reading aloud, Sunday after Sunday, that they trusted as coming from the apostles and their circle, and that matched the faith they'd been taught, came to be called scripture. You can watch it start inside the Bible itself. The second letter of Peter talks about Paul's letters, which some people twist, "as they do also the other scriptures." Paul's mail, set beside the scriptures. Over time, bishops and councils wrote the books down in lists. One that survives is a letter from Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent to his churches at Easter. He names the books of both testaments and calls them fountains of salvation, adding that no one should add to them or take from them. And there's a real difference between churches today. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books such as Tobit and the Maccabees in the Old Testament; Protestant Bibles leave them out or print them apart, as the Apocrypha. Catholics and Orthodox stress the church recognizing the books. Protestants stress the books carrying their own authority, which the church came to see. Both say the church didn't invent the Bible. It listened, and kept reading.

Here's the practice: look at one list of books. If there's a Bible nearby, open it to the contents page. If not, a Bible app or a search will show you one. That page is a list, like the one Athanasius sent his churches. Settle, and breathe. Then read the names slowly, one at a time. Genesis. Ruth. Psalms. Mark. Romans. Some will be familiar, some strangers. Each name was read aloud in rooms full of people long before it was printed on that page. If you pray, you can give thanks for the readers. If not, just let the names go by. The bell holds the time.
How the Bible was gathered: not voted into being in one afternoon, but read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs, and then written down in lists.

fork.setup: you're in an early church, and a letter from an apostle has just been read aloud to your congregation. what happens to it next?
options: it's locked away so no one else sees it.
it's sent on down the road to be read in another church.
it's burned, since everyone has heard it now.
fork.reveal: Paul tells the Colossians to send their letter on to Laodicea and read the one coming from there. sharing and reading aloud is how the books traveled.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible was always one book.
what it means: letters and gospels read aloud in worship, kept, shared, and in time written down in lists by bishops and councils.

what a scholar hears: the list is called the canon, a word usually explained as a measuring rule. Athanasius's Easter letter is one early list; Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant lists still differ on some Old Testament books.

notes: Audit (fresh reviewer): all KJV/BCP quotations checked word for word, attributions and framing checked; no change needed.

Claims rule: the outline hook's 'over centuries' and 'around the fourth century' are cut; no dates or book counts are given. Athanasius's Festal Letter 39 (367) is named without a date. The teaser hook is rewritten without dates.

'Fountains of salvation' and 'let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these' paraphrase Athanasius (Festal Letter 39, NPNF translation); not quoted because the exact wording wasn't verified. Confirm.

Colossians 4:16 is paraphrased in the hook. 'From the apostles and their circle' and 'matched the faith they'd been taught' summarize the usual criteria (apostolicity, orthodoxy, use in worship); confirm the summary.

Catholic/Orthodox vs Protestant canon: Tobit and Maccabees named as examples. Orthodox canons include further books; kept general. 'Both say the church didn't invent the Bible' – confirm as fair for both.
Trapdoor: 'canon' as a measuring rule is an etymology, attributed ('usually explained'). Confirm or cut.
